1G (Linear Algebra)

Words: 262 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 262
1G OurBigBook.com
The Steinitz exchange lemma says that if u1​,…,ur​ are linearly independent and v1​,…,vs​ span the same vector space, then r≤s and, after reordering the vj​, the list u1​,…,ur​,vr+1​,…,vs​ still spans it.
To prove this, suppose u1​,…,uk​ have already replaced k of the spanning vectors. Express uk+1​ in that spanning list. At least one coefficient of an unreplaced vj​ is nonzero: otherwise uk+1​ lies in the span of u1​,…,uk​, contradicting linear independence. Solve this expression for that vj​ and replace it by uk+1​. The new list still spans. If all s vectors were replaced before the ui​ were exhausted, the next ui​ would be dependent on its predecessors. Hence r≤s, and the replacement can continue through ur​.
For two bases of sizes r,s, apply the Steinitz exchange lemma in both directions to get r≤s≤r. Thus every basis has the same size. Given a linearly independent set and any finite basis, the replacement procedure produces a finite spanning list containing that set. Successively delete any remaining vector dependent on the others; none of the prescribed independent vectors need be deleted, since one can instead delete a dependent supplementary vector. Equivalently, greedily retain only supplementary vectors outside the span already built. The resulting list is a basis containing the prescribed set.
For the three-dimensional example, the columns have matrix
A3​=​110​011​101​​,detA3​=2.
(1)
Therefore the three vectors are a basis. For the four-dimensional example,
(e1​+e2​)−(e2​+e3​)+(e3​+e4​)−(e4​+e1​)=0.
(2)
This is a nontrivial linear dependence, so the four vectors are not a basis. The distinction is an instance of the adjacent sums of a cyclic basis criterion: alternating coefficients close consistently around an even cycle, but not an odd one.

Let the regular curves be zj​(t) with zj​(0)=z0​ and nonzero tangent vectors aj​=zj′​(0). By the chain rule, their transformed tangents are f′(z0​)aj​. Multiplication by the nonzero complex number f′(z0​)=ρeiα scales both tangent lengths by ρ and rotates both directions by α. In particular,
argf′(z0​)a1​f′(z0​)a2​​=arga1​a2​​.
(3)
Thus the oriented angle, and hence the ordinary angle, is unchanged. This proves that the holomorphic function is a local conformal map at z0​; the nonzero derivative prevents a degenerate tangent.
A suitable conformal inversion of a quadrant is
f(z)=−z1​.​
(4)
If z=reiθ with 0<r<1 and π/2<θ<π, then f(z)=r−1ei(π−θ) has modulus greater than one and argument strictly between zero and π/2. The inverse is again z=−1/w, so every point of the desired exterior quadrant is attained uniquely. The origin is outside the open source region, and f′(z)=1/z2=0 there.

σu​=(−bsinucosv,−bsinusinv,bcosu),σv​=(−Rsinv,Rcosv,0).

Their squared lengths and inner product give the first fundamental form
I=b2du2+R2dv2.

The unit normal determined by this ordered parametrization is
ν=∣σu​×σv​∣σu​×σv​​=−(cosucosv,cosusinv,sinu).

Taking inner products of ν with σuu​, σuv​ and σvv​ yields e=b, f=0, g=Rcosu. Consequently the second fundamental form of a ring torus is
II=bdu2+(a+bcosu)cosudv2.​

This normal points into the tube. Choosing the outward unit normal reverses both coefficients and gives −II; the choice must therefore accompany an answer for the second fundamental form.
The Gaussian curvature is unchanged by that reversal:
K=EG−F2eg−f2​=b(a+bcosu)cosu​.​

Since the denominator is positive, K>0 on the outside of the torus, where cosu>0, and K<0 on its inner side, where cosu<0. It vanishes on the two circles u=π/2,3π/2. This is the Gaussian curvature of a ring torus.

5B (Fluid Dynamics)

Words: 144 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 144
5B OurBigBook.com
Take a steady parallel velocity (u(y),0) and interpret the specified gradient as px​=G>0. The horizontal Navier-Stokes equation reduces to μu′′=G: the pressure force opposes positive x motion. The no-slip boundary condition imposes u(0)=0, u(h)=U. Integrating twice gives
u(y)=−2μG​y(h−y)+hUy​.​
(15)
The velocity gradient is u′=G(y−h/2)/μ+U/h, an increasing function of y. It is negative somewhere in the channel exactly when its lower-wall limit is negative:
G>h22μU​.​
(16)
Under this condition the negative-gradient interval is 0<y<h/2−μU/(Gh).
The volume flux per unit span is
Q=∫0h​u(y)dy=−12μGh3​+2Uh​.
(17)
Thus the zero-flux Couette-Poiseuille flow requires
G=h26μU​,Uu​=3s2−2s,s=y/h.​
(18)
The profile starts at zero, reaches u=−U/3 at y=h/3, crosses zero at y=2h/3, and reaches U at the moving wall. Negative and positive flux contributions cancel, even though the local velocity is nonzero.

Insert an exact smooth solution into the linear multistep method and define its unscaled local truncation error by
Rh​[y]=∑ℓ=0s​ρℓ​y(t+ℓh)−h∑ℓ=0s​σℓ​y′(t+ℓh).
(19)
Its Taylor expansion has coefficients
Rh​[y]=c0​y(t)+∑j≥1​cj​hjy(j)(t),c0​=∑ℓ​ρℓ​,cj​=j!1​∑ℓ​ℓjρℓ​−(j−1)!1​∑ℓ​ℓj−1σℓ​.
(20)
The method has order at least p exactly when c0​=⋯=cp​=0, since then Rh​[y]=O(hp+1) for every sufficiently smooth y. Necessity can be checked by inserting polynomials of successive degrees. This also corresponds to the usual truncation error Rh​/h=O(hp).
On the other hand, expansion of the characteristic polynomials of a linear multistep method gives
ρ(ez)−zσ(ez)=c0​+c1​z+c2​z2+⋯.
(21)
Thus the exponential-symbol order criterion for a multistep method is
ρ(ez)−zσ(ez)=O(zp+1) ⟺ order at least p.​
(22)
If “order p” is meant to be the exact rather than guaranteed order, one additionally requires cp+1​=0. The first two vanishing conditions are the usual consistency of a numerical method relations ρ(1)=0, ρ′(1)=σ(1).

ii

Words: 191 Articles: 1

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
The relevant one of the characteristic polynomials of a linear multistep method is
ρ(w)=w3+(a−1)w−a=(w−1)(w2+w+a).
(23)
The coefficients on the right are chosen to give third order, so consistency of a numerical method is already available. By the Dahlquist equivalence theorem, convergence with convergent starting values is equivalent to zero-stability: every root of ρ must satisfy ∣w∣≤1, and every root on the unit circle must be simple.
If a<0, the quadratic is negative at w=−1 and tends to +∞ as w→−∞, so it has a root less than −1. If a>1, its root product is a, so at least one root has modulus greater than one. For 0≤a≤1/4, its real roots (−1±1−4a​)/2 lie in [−1,0]. For 1/4<a≤1, its conjugate roots have modulus a​≤1.
At a=0, the three roots are 1,0,−1, with the unit-modulus roots simple. At a=1, they are 1,e2πi/3,e−2πi/3, again simple. The repeated quadratic root at a=1/4 is −1/2, strictly inside the unit circle, which the root condition for a multistep method permits. Therefore
the method is convergent exactly for 0≤a≤1.​
(24)
This is the root stability of a cubic multistep polynomial; oscillatory parasitic roots at the endpoints do not invalidate convergence when their starting amplitudes tend to zero.

A useful form of the Lagrangian sufficiency theorem is as follows. For minimization of f(x) subject to gj​(x)≥0 and hi​(x)=0, form
L(x,λ,ν)=f(x)−∑j​λj​gj​(x)+∑i​νi​hi​(x).
(31)
If x∗​ is feasible, λj​≥0, λj​gj​(x∗​)=0, and x∗​ globally minimizes L over the ambient domain for these fixed multipliers, then x∗​ is a global constrained minimizer. Indeed, for every feasible x,
f(x)≥L(x,λ,ν)≥L(x∗​,λ,ν)=f(x∗​).
(32)
The first inequality uses multiplier signs; the last equality uses feasibility and complementary slackness. Equality constraints alone require no sign restriction on their multipliers. A stationary point of a differentiable convex Lagrangian is a global minimum, which is a common way to verify the theorem's hypothesis.
Here take
L=2x12​+2x22​+x32​−λ(x1​+x2​+x3​−1).
(33)
Stationarity gives 4x1​=4x2​=2x3​=λ. Feasibility then gives λ=1 and x∗​=(1/4,1/4,1/2). For that multiplier,
L=2(x1​−1/4)2+2(x2​−1/4)2+(x3​−1/2)2+21​.
(34)
The Lagrangian has its unique global minimum at x∗​, so the sufficiency theorem proves
x∗​=(1/4,1/4,1/2),minf=1/2.​
(35)

i OurBigBook.com
If x=0, the generated subspace is zero and invariant. Otherwise, let r be the first index for which x,Tx,…,Trx are linearly dependent. Such an index exists with 1≤r≤n, since there are n+1 vectors. The preceding vectors are independent, so the coefficient of Trx in this first relation cannot vanish. Hence
Trx∈span{x,Tx,…,Tr−1x}.
(36)
The linear operator T sends each of the first r−1 generators to the next and sends the last into their span. This proves that their span is an invariant subspace. Every later iterate lies in the same subspace by induction, so it equals the span of the first n iterates. Therefore the indicated subspace is T-invariant. This proof of a cyclic subspace uses only finite dimension and linear dependence.

Expanding det(tI−C) along its last column gives
χT​(t)=tn+an−1​tn−1+⋯+a1​t+a0​.

Induct on n. The one-dimensional assertion is immediate, and the zero-dimensional case is vacuous. If T has a cyclic vector spanning all of V, the direct proof in part (ii) applies. Otherwise choose x=0 and let W be its cyclic subspace. Part (i) makes W invariant; the absence of a cyclic vector makes it proper and nonzero.
By induction, the restriction to W is annihilated by χA​, and the induced map on V/W is annihilated by χD​. The quotient assertion means χD​(T)V⊂W. Applying the restriction assertion next gives
χA​(T)χD​(T)V=0.
(44)
By the characteristic factorization in part (iii), this is precisely χT​(T)V=0. Hence
χT​(T)=0for every finite-dimensional endomorphism.​
(45)
This is the Cayley-Hamilton theorem from cyclic subspaces; using the quotient map is what makes the argument valid even when the block B is nonzero.

10E (Groups, Rings and Modules)

Words: 252 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 252
10E OurBigBook.com
If ∣G∣=pam with p∤m, a Sylow subgroup for p is a subgroup of order pa. The Sylow theorems assert: such subgroups exist; every p-subgroup is contained in a Sylow subgroup; all Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate; and their number np​ divides m and satisfies np​≡1(modp).
For groups of order p squared q are not simple, if p>q, then np​∣q and np​≡1(modp) force np​=1. Its unique Sylow subgroup is a nontrivial proper normal subgroup. Suppose instead p<q. If either Sylow count is one, the conclusion already follows. Otherwise np​=q, while nq​ is either p or p2. The value p is impossible because 0<p−1<q. Thus nq​=p2, and q∣(p2−1)=(p−1)(p+1). Primality and q>p imply q∣p+1, hence q=p+1. The only consecutive primes are p=2,q=3.
In that exceptional order-12 case, four distinct Sylow 3-subgroups contribute eight distinct nonidentity elements: their intersections are trivial. Only three nonidentity elements remain. Every subgroup of order four must contain exactly those remaining three, so there can be only one Sylow 2-subgroup, contradicting the assumption that both counts were nontrivial. Therefore no group of order p2q with distinct primes is simple.
For the final factorization, normality of H ensures g−1Pg is a Sylow p-subgroup of H. By Sylow conjugacy within H, choose h∈H such that g−1Pg=h−1Ph. Then k=gh−1 satisfies
kPk−1=gh−1Phg−1=P.
(46)
Thus k∈NG​(P) and g=kh. We have proved the Frattini argument
G=NG​(P)H.​
(47)
The normaliser factorization includes the case P={1}, when its normalizer is all of G.

Two Lipschitz equivalent norms N1​,N2​ satisfy cN1​(v)≤N2​(v)≤CN1​(v) for all v, for constants 0<c≤C<∞. These inequalities give the same convergent sequences in both norms. A subset of a metric space is closed exactly when it contains the limits of all convergent sequences from that subset. Therefore closedness is the same in the two norms.
For finite dimension, fix a basis e1​,…,ed​ and let x=∑j​xj​ej​. For any norm N,
N(x)≤∑j​∣xj​∣N(ej​)≤C(∑j​xj2​)1/2.
(48)
The reverse triangle inequality then makes N continuous in the Euclidean coordinate norm. If no positive lower bound existed on the Euclidean unit sphere, choose xm​ there with N(xm​)→0. By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, a subsequence converges to x on the unit sphere. Continuity would give N(x)=0, although x=0, a contradiction. Thus N is bounded below by a positive multiple of the Euclidean norm. Comparing any two norms through that coordinate norm proves all norms in finite dimension are Lipschitz equivalent.
On C[0,1], nonnegativity, absolute homogeneity and the triangle inequality for ∥f∥1​=∫01​∣f∣ follow from the corresponding real-number properties and integration. If a continuous f is nonzero at a point, it has absolute value bounded below by a positive constant on a nontrivial one-sided or two-sided interval around that point. Its integral is then positive. Hence ∥f∥1​=0 implies f=0, completing the norm axioms.
For n≥2, put gn​(x)=max{1−n∣x−1/2∣,0} and fn​=1−gn​. Then fn​(1/2)=0, but
∥fn​−1∥1​=∫01​gn​(x)dx=n1​⟶0.
(49)
The limit function 1 is not in the indicated point evaluation kernel. Consequently that set is not closed in the integral norm. This is the point-evaluation kernel is not closed in the integral norm phenomenon.
Finally ∥gn​∥∞​=1 while ∥gn​∥1​=1/n. Thus no constant can bound the uniform norm by a multiple of the integral norm. Although ∥f∥1​≤∥f∥∞​ on this unit interval, the converse comparison fails: the two norms are not Lipschitz equivalent. The finite-dimensional theorem cannot be applied to this infinite-dimensional function space.

12E (Metric and Topological Spaces)

Words: 248 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 248
12E OurBigBook.com
A compact space is one for which every open cover has a finite subcover. A Hausdorff space has disjoint open neighbourhoods of any two distinct points.
Let K be a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space X, and let x∈/K. For each y∈K, choose disjoint open neighbourhoods Uy​ of y and Vy​ of x. Finitely many Uy1​​,…,Uym​​ cover K. Their corresponding intersection Vy1​​∩⋯∩Vym​​ is an open neighbourhood of x disjoint from K. Thus X∖K is open, proving compact subspaces of a Hausdorff space are closed.
In particular, C1​∩C2​ is closed as a subspace of compact C1​. A closed subset of a compact space is compact: add its open complement to an open cover, apply compactness to the whole space, and discard that extra open set. Hence C1​∩C2​ is compact.
In the cocountable topology on R, two nonempty open sets always intersect. Their two countable complements have countable union, which cannot exhaust the uncountable real line. Therefore this space is not Hausdorff.
Every finite subset is compact in any topology. Conversely, from any infinite subset C select distinct points c1​,c2​,… and define
Un​=R∖{cj​:j≥n}.
(50)
Each Un​ is cocountable and open; the sets increase and their union is all of R. They therefore cover C, but a finite selection is contained in some UN​, which misses the infinitely many cj​ with j≥N. No finite subcover exists. Thus the compact subsets of a cocountable space are
exactly the finite subsets.​
(51)

Substitute y(x)=∑j≥0​cj​xj into the Legendre differential equation. Matching the coefficient of xj gives
cj+2​=(j+2)(j+1)j(j+1)−n(n+1)​cj​.​
(57)
Choose the parity of n: start with nonzero c0​ for even n, or nonzero c1​ for odd n, and set the other parity to zero. The numerator is nonzero for every preceding index of that parity below n, so cn​=0, but at j=n it vanishes. All higher coefficients are zero. This constructs a nonzero polynomial solution of degree exactly n.
Its value at x=1 cannot be zero. If it had a zero there of multiplicity k≥1, write y=(x−1)kR with R(1)=0. The lowest-order term of (1−x2)y′′−2xy′ would be −2k2R(1)(x−1)k−1, whereas n(n+1)y starts at order k. The differential equation could not hold. Hence the polynomial can be scaled to satisfy Pn​(1)=1.
The resulting Legendre polynomials begin
P0​(x)=1,P1​(x)=x,P2​(x)=21​(3x2−1).​
(58)
Each satisfies both the differential equation and the specified normalization.

Set U=R(r)Θ(θ) in the Laplace equation, multiply by r2/U, and separate:
R1​(r2R′)′=λ,sinθ1​(sinθΘ′)′+λΘ=0.
(59)
Putting x=cosθ turns the angular equation into the Legendre differential equation. For a solution smooth on the whole spherical axis, the allowed eigenvalues are λ=n(n+1) with angular functions Pn​(cosθ). The radial equation has the two solutions rn,r−n−1. Superposition yields the regular axisymmetric expansion
U(r,θ)=n=0∑∞​(An​rn+Bn​r−n−1)Pn​(cosθ).​
(60)
The coefficients and convergence region are set by the domain and boundary data. Without regularity at the poles, singular Legendre functions and more general separated degrees would also be possible; they are excluded for this exterior spherical field.
The far-field matching fixes A1​=v0​ and all other growing coefficients to zero. The radial Neumann boundary condition at r0​ is
∑n=0∞​[nAn​r0n−1​−(n+1)Bn​r0−n−2​]Pn​(cosθ)=0.
(61)
Independence of the angular modes gives B1​=v0​r03​/2 and all other decaying coefficients zero. Thus the exterior harmonic potential with no flux through a sphere is
U=v0​(r+2r2r03​​)cosθ.​
(62)
Its derivative vanishes on the sphere and its difference from v0​rcosθ tends to zero at infinity. A spatial constant may be added if the far-field condition is intended only to specify the gradient or the leading growing term; matching the potential difference to zero fixes that constant to zero.

αn​=a​1​.​

The stationary states vanish at both walls and form an orthonormal basis of the square-integrable state space. A common arbitrary phase on each basis function does not alter any energy or measurement probability.

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
An ideal conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has zero field in its interior and constant potential on its surface. Grounding fixes that potential to zero. The tangential field is continuous and therefore vanishes; the normal field has the jump fixed by the induced surface charge density σ:
Ex​=Ey​=0(z=0+),Ez​(0+)=ε0​σ​,E(0−)=0.​
(74)
Here the normal points upward out of the conductor. The normal field is not generally zero; grounding prescribes the potential, not the induced charge density.

ii

Words: 121 Articles: 1
16A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 121
ii OurBigBook.com
The method of images places an image charge −q at the reflected position below the plane. The candidate potential in the physical upper half-space is
Φ=4πε0​q​[x2+y2+(z−d)2​1​−x2+y2+(z+d)2​1​].
(75)
At z=0 the two terms cancel, so Φ=0 and Ex​=Ey​=0. Direct differentiation gives
Ez​(0+)=−2πε0​(x2+y2+d2)3/2qd​,σ=−2π(x2+y2+d2)3/2qd​.
(76)
Thus the upper-side field satisfies exactly the conductor boundary conditions from part (i). The fictitious pair does have a field below the plane, but that part of its solution is not used for the physical conductor.
In z>0, the potential has the correct real point source, the correct zero Dirichlet boundary condition, and the required decay at infinity. By Uniqueness of the Dirichlet problem, it is the physical potential there. This is why the artificial charge can represent the induced conductor response without being a second physical charge.

mz¨=−4πε0​(2z)2q2​,z¨=−z2κ​,κ=16πε0​mq2​.
(77)
The image is not kept at its initial position. Multiplying by z˙ and using z(0)=d, z˙(0)=0 gives
21​z˙2=κ(z1​−d1​),z˙<0.
(78)
For the falling charge above a grounded conducting plane, the arrival time is
T=2κ​1​∫0d​1/z−1/d​dz​.

Put z=dsin2θ; the integral becomes 2d3/2∫0π/2​sin2θdθ=πd3/2/2. Hence
T=22κ​πd3/2​=∣q∣π​2πε0​md3​.​

This is the finite arrival time in the specified ideal force model, for q=0. The field-force derivation also avoids incorrectly using the full real-image pair interaction energy: the conductor's effective energy is −q2/(16πε0​z), with the factor one-half appropriate to induced charge.

The steady Euler equations for an inviscid fluid with no body force are (u⋅∇)u=−∇p/ρ. Use the convective acceleration identity
(u⋅∇)u=∇(21​∣u∣2)−u×(∇×u)

to obtain
u×ω=∇(ρp​+21​∣u∣2).​

For the question's streamfunction convention, u=(ψy​,−ψx​,0), so u×ω=−ω∇ψ. Constant ω therefore gives the Bernoulli function for planar constant-vorticity flow
21​∣u∣2+ωψ+p/ρ=C​

on the connected fluid region.
For circular streamlines, write u=w(r)ϕ​. The cylindrical curl gives (rw)′/r=ω, so w=ωr/2+C1​/r. The outer wall condition gives C1​=−2ωa2. Choose the positive azimuthal orientation so that w(a)=V, as implicit in the requested sign for ω. Then
ω=−3a2V​,u=3aV​(r4a2​−r)ϕ​.​

Reversing the circulation reverses ω but leaves the speed and pressure difference unchanged. For this uniform-vorticity circular flow in an annulus, one convenient streamfunction is ψ=V(r2/2−4a2log(r/a))/(3a)+C2​.
The radial component of the Euler equations for an inviscid fluid is pr​=ρw2/r. Thus pressure increases outwards, and
p(2a)−p(a)​=9a2ρV2​∫a2a​(r316a4​−r8a2​+r)dr=9a2ρV2​[215a2​−8a2log2].​

Therefore
Δp=p(2a)−p(a)=1815−16log2​ρV2.​

For a nonzero real vector v, the Householder transformation is
H=I−2vTvvvT​.
(87)
Writing P=vvT/(vTv) gives PT=P, P2=P, so HT=H and HTH=(I−2P)2=I. Thus H is orthogonal. It reverses the component along v and fixes its orthogonal complement.
For Householder QR decomposition, successively choose a reflector on each trailing row block to send its current column to a multiple of the first coordinate vector. Each step annihilates the subdiagonal entries without disturbing earlier columns. The reflector product gives an upper-trapezoidal R and its transpose gives an orthogonal Q with A=QR.
Here the first column has norm four. Taking v=(−1,1,−1,1)T gives H1​=I−vvT/2 and
H1​A=​4000​4600​8−3912​​.
(88)
The second column already has no unwanted entries. On the last two rows, reflect using (−1,2)T:
B=I2​−52​(1−2​−24​)=(3/54/5​4/5−3/5​),H3​=diag(I2​,B).
(89)
This maps (9,12)T to (15,0)T. Therefore a full QR factorization is
R=​4000​4600​8−3150​​,Q=H1​H3​=101​​55−55​555−5​1−177​−7711​​.​
(90)
Both displayed factors arise from the explicit reflectors; in particular QTQ=I4​ and QR=A.
The first three diagonal entries of R are nonzero, so the column rank is three and a consistent system has a unique solution. Consistency requires the last component of QTb to vanish. For the given right side this component is
101​[−7(1+λ)+7⋅2+3+4]=107​(2−λ).
(91)
Hence
λ=2.​
(92)
For this value the transformed right side is (3,2,5,0)T. Back substitution also gives x=(−5/12,1/2,1/3)T. This illustrates the Householder reduction of an overdetermined consistent system.

L(1)L(θ1​)​=e−3(θ1​−1)θ1S​.

Since θ1​>1, this is strictly increasing in S. A threshold chosen between its values at S=5 and S=6 gives precisely the stated upper-tail critical region, so it is a likelihood-ratio test.
The sum has a Poisson distribution with mean 3θ. Thus the size of a statistical test and its statistical power at θ1​ are
α=1−e−3j=0∑5​j!3j​=1−F3​(5)≃0.084,power(θ1​)=1−e−3θ1​j=0∑5​j!(3θ1​)j​.​
(94)
For the grouped-area problem, let S1​=∑i=1m​Yi​, S2​=∑i=m+12m​Yi​, T=S1​+S2​. The null log likelihood, up to data-only constants, is
ℓ0​(λ)=−3maλ+Tlogλ+Tloga+S2​log2.
(95)
The maximum-likelihood estimate is λ=T/(3ma), giving fitted means T/(3m) and 2T/(3m) in the two groups. Under the alternative, the fitted group means are λ1​=S1​/m and λ2​=S2​/m.
Use the increasing generalized likelihood-ratio test convention Λ=supH1​​L/supH0​​L≥1, consistent with the printed positive 2logΛ. The exponential and factorial factors cancel, yielding the likelihood-ratio test of area-proportional Poisson means
Λ=(T3S1​​)S1​(2T3S2​​)S2​,2logΛ=2[S1​logT3S1​​+S2​log2T3S2​​].​
(96)
Terms with zero count are interpreted as 0log0=0; if T=0, take Λ=1. If the inverse ratio is used, the reported test statistic is instead −2logΛ.
Under the null, the regular large-sample Wilks theorem approximation is 2logΛ∼χ12​: the alternative has two rate parameters and the null one. The value 15.67 far exceeds the usual 1% critical value, about 6.63, and has approximate tail probability 7.5×10−5. Thus reject proportionality of the expected counts to area: the two groups show evidence of different territory densities. The statistic alone does not say which group has greater density; that requires S1​/m versus S2​/(2m). For small counts, an exact conditional test uses S1​∣T∼Binomial(T,1/3) under the null instead of the asymptotic calibration.

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
For a state i, its period is di​=gcd{n≥1:pii(n)​>0}; the condition di​=1 defines aperiodicity. It is a positive recurrent state if return occurs almost surely and its first strictly positive return time has finite expectation. An ergodic state of a Markov chain is positive recurrent and aperiodic.
The PDF specifies pi,i−1​=1 for i≥1; the TeX aid drops the essential value one. Consequently every positive state reaches zero deterministically. From zero, every positive state j is reached in one step with probability pqj−1>0. Paths through zero connect any pair of states, proving irreducibility.
Let J be the jump out of zero. It has P(J=j)=pqj−1 for j≥1, after which exactly j downward steps return to zero. Therefore T0​=J+1, giving
P0​(T0​=n)={0,pqn−2,​n=1,n≥2.​​
(97)
These probabilities sum to one and
E0​T0​=1+1/p=(1+p)/p.​
(98)
Returns of lengths two and three both have positive probability, so the period is one. Hence state zero is ergodic, and by irreducibility all states are positive recurrent and have the same period.
For this geometric-jump countdown Markov chain, the invariant equations give π0​=π1​ and πj​=πj+1​+π0​pqj−1 for j≥1. Summing the tail, or counting visits in a regeneration cycle, yields πj​=π0​qj−1. Normalization gives
π0​=1+pp​,πj​=1+pp​qj−1(j≥1).​
(99)
This is the stationary distribution of a regenerative countdown chain. The standard recurrence identity for an irreducible positive recurrent Markov chain is Ei​Ti+​=1/πi​, so
Ei​Ti+​=pqi−11+p​(i≥1).​
(100)

n→∞lim​P0​(Xn​=0)=1−π0​=1+p1​.​

Although p00​=0, the chain is aperiodic because its possible return lengths have greatest common divisor one; a self-loop is sufficient but not necessary for aperiodicity.
